cards.b: Develop ideas through investigation, demonstrating critical understanding. 25 of 100 marks in each component.
Looking closely at artists' work, explaining how and why it works, and using it to develop your own ideas.
Evidence you make or see yourself: your own drawings, photographs, gallery visits.
Images and information made by others: books, magazines, websites.
An artist, art movement, historical event or local/national art, craft or design that gives your work a background.

cards.f: Study in the style of an artist
cards.b: Your own piece that copies a method to learn from it, then applies it to your subject. Not tracing.
About three to five across a project, with at least one living or recent artist.
The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c.1831): Japanese woodblock print with strong outline and flat colour.
Thick directional brush marks (impasto) and intense colour, e.g. The Starry Night (1889).
Mexican painter of symbolic self-portraits about identity, pain and culture.
Japanese artist known for polka dots, repetition and Infinity Mirror Rooms.
American artist (1960-1988): raw scribbled lines, words and symbols; started as a graffiti artist.
British sculptor of body casts and the Angel of the North (1998). Useful for form, figure and scale.
Names the artist's feature and says how you used it in your own theme, e.g. repetition to show a busy city.
Using others' work without citing it is plagiarism; the syllabus requires proper citation.

gaps.s: Your own drawings and photographs are ___ sources.
Using someone else's work without crediting it is ___.
A piece that copies an artist's method to learn from it is a ___ in their style.
Annotation, if used, must be relevant, purposeful and written in ___.
The Great Wave off Kanagawa was made by ___.
AO3 is worth ___ marks in each component.

short.model: It means looking carefully at an artist's work, explaining how and why it works, and using that to develop your own ideas.

short.q: Describe how to make a study in the style of an artist.
short.model: Choose a small part of the work, use similar materials, note what you found hard, then apply the method to your own subject.

short.q: Why are gallery visits useful for research?
short.model: You see real scale, colour and surface, and can make first-hand sketches and notes that you can use to change your own work.

short.q: Why is a pasted biography weak evidence?
short.model: It shows no thinking of your own: no analysis, no study and no link to your idea, so it earns little for AO3.

short.q: Give a strong link sentence for Kusama.
short.model: Kusama repeats one shape to fill space, so I repeated bus tickets to show the rush of city life.
